newsitem.title: TANZANIA: U.N. Rwanda trial hears BBC journalist's evidence.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Rwanda trial hears BBC journalist's evidence.

text.p: A British foreign correspondent testified on Friday that she saw a pile of bodies "like a mountain" in the Rwandan capital Kigali at the start of the slaughter of Tutsis by Hutu militia and mobs in 1994.

Lindsey Hilsum, working for the British Broadcasting Corporation at the time, was testifying at the United Nations tribunal for Rwanda, which is hearing cases against key suspects behind the genocide of Tutsis and killings of moderate Hutus.
Hilsum was one of the few correspondents in Kigali on April 6, 1994, when the mass killings began. She told the court she saw aound 500 bodies outside Kigali central hospital.
"There was a big pile like a mountain outside and these were bodies with slash wounds, with heads smashed in, many of them were naked," she said.
Hilsum, the prosecution's fifth witness and the second expert to testify, did not mention in her testimony the accused, Jean-Paul Akayesu.
But her evidence is key to the prosecution, which must prove Akayesu, 43, participated in a genocide.

Akayesu, the former mayor of Rwanda's central Taba commune, has pleaded not guilty to charges of genocide and crimes against humanity. If convicted he faces life imprisonment, the tribunal's higest penalty.

Rwanda's genocide of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus was sparked off by the assassination of Hutu president and military strongman Juvenal Habyarimana on April 6, 1994 as he returned from a regional peace summit in Tanzania.
Angry Hutu followers including his militia and soldiers took up arms and hunted down Tutsis and Hutus opposed to his junta.
Hilsum said on the evening of April 6 she heard two loud explosions coming from the direction of the airport and later learned that Habyarimana's plane had been shot down.
She said soldiers prevented her from leaving her house for more than a day after April 6, but she finally ventured out in a car.
"I knew I had to get out and see with my own eyes what was happening," said Hilsum, who arrived in Rwanda in February 1994 on contract with the U.N. Children's Fund.
During a tour of the city she followed-up reports of killings close to a depot for the Belgium Red Cross and found corpses by a house guarded by two soldiers.
"I saw the bodies of five women piled up in a flowerbed and I would say that this was one of the most horrific things I had ever seen up to that point in my life," she said.
"They had machete wounds, they were slashed across their necks, across their arms, across their heads, the blood was still fresh and there were flies crawling all over them," she said.
Akayesu sat impassively behind a screen during the hearing flanked by two security guards.
Hilsum's testimony on Kigali followed evidence by a doctor for aid agency Doctors Without Borders, who said he saw hundreds of corpses and scores of killings in southern Rwanda in April 1994.
Akayesu is the first to be tried before the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, set up in November 1994.
Earlier, three witnesses from Taba told the court Akayesu ordered killings of Tutsis and two said he beat and tortured them.
The next witness is expected to be a TV cameraman who worked in northern Rwanda during the genocide.
A total of 21 people have been indicted by the tribunal of whom seven are in custody at tribunal headquarters in northern Tanzania.
Rwanda has also started its own separate trials of some genocide suspects. Up to 90,000 people are being held in prisons across the tiny tea and coffee-growing nation.
